articles.title: Remembrance Sunday: parades and services at eight war memorials across Rochdale borough
articles.excerpt: Times and routes for today's Remembrance Sunday parades in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle.
articles.content_html:
Veterans, serving personnel and civic leaders are marching to eight war memorials across the Rochdale borough today for Remembrance Sunday parades and services.

Parades and services are being held in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle on Sunday 8 November. Representatives of the Royal Navy, the Army and the Royal Air Force are joining veterans and civic dignitaries, according to Rochdale Borough Council.

Everyone is welcome at the services and no booking is needed.

Rochdale: the parade assembles at 10.30am outside the Flying Horse Hotel on Packer Street, where ward councillors, magistrates and other civic guests join at 10.45am. It sets off at 10.50am through the pedestrian area to the Cenotaph in Rochdale Memorial Gardens, for a service at 10.55am followed by a march past. The parade then returns to the Flying Horse Hotel and disperses.

In Rochdale this morning, standard bearers, veterans, Army, Air and Sea Cadets, Beavers and a youth band marched from the Flying Horse Hotel to the Cenotaph, where crowds gathered for the service.

Heywood: the parade assembles at 10.15am on Tower Street and moves to St James' Street at 10.30am. It marches along Bridge Street, Market Street, Market Place and Hind Hill Street to Heywood Memorial Gardens on Church Street, arriving at 10.45am, for a service at 10.55am.

At 11.20am the Heywood parade leaves via Hind Hill Street, Pine Street and Hornby Street to Church Street, where the salute is taken, before returning through Market Place, Market Street, Bridge Street and St James' Street to Tower Street.

Middleton: the parade assembles at 10.10am outside the Wetherspoon pub on Long Street and leaves at 10.20am for Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road. The service begins at 10.45am.

Littleborough: the parade assembles at 10.15am at Hare Hill Park and leaves at 10.30am for Littleborough War Memorial, at the Church Street and Railway Street crossroads. The service is at 10.55am, and the parade returns to Hare Hill Park at about 11.35am.

Milnrow: the parade assembles at 10.25am on Harmony Street, moves to Milnrow Library at 10.35am and leaves at 10.45am for the memorial on Newhey Road. The service is at 10.55am, and the parade returns to Harmony Street at 11.20am.

Castleton: a service is held at 10.50am at Castleton Memorial Gardens on Queensway.

Norden: a service is held at 10.50am at Norden Memorial Gardens, at the junction of Edenfield Road and Woodhouse Lane. Part of Woodhouse Lane is closed for 45 metres from its junction with Shawfield Lane.

Wardle: the borough's only afternoon parade assembles at 2.15pm in Village Square and leaves at 2.30pm for the War Memorial on Wardle Road. The service is at 3pm, and the parade returns to Village Square at 3.30pm.

The council has also closed roads for the parades in Heywood, Middleton, Milnrow and Wardle, and has said no alternative routes are provided for some of them while the parades pass.

Mayor of Rochdale Councillor Faisal Rana said: "We are united in our remembrance. Lest we forget."

St Luke's Church in Deeplish is holding a Remembrance service of Holy Communion at 10.30am, led by Revd Natty Gray.

The Royal British Legion's Poppy Appeal ends today. Poppies are available on the Legion's website, at Number One Riverside in Rochdale and at outlets across the borough.

Remembrance events in the borough began with the Festival of Remembrance at Rochdale Town Hall on 16 October. Walkers from Get Together After Serving also completed a 22-mile walk past eight of the borough's cenotaphs to raise money for veterans.

Armistice Day falls on Wednesday 11 November, with the national two-minute silence at 11am. Questions about the parades can be sent to the council at ArmedForces@rochdale.gov.uk.

articles.title: Drunk driver jailed after Rochdale police pursuit left pedestrian with life-changing injuries
articles.excerpt: Cameron Grainger fled officers through Rochdale town centre after a night drinking. A man was seriously injured when he was struck by the police car trying to stop him.
articles.content_html:
A man who led police on a pursuit through Rochdale after an evening of drinking has been jailed for more than four years.

Cameron Grainger was found guilty of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court today (Friday 6 November), Greater Manchester Police said. He was also banned from driving for six years and two months.

The court heard that at about 1am on Sunday 19 November 2023, Grainger parked his Seat Leon in the Upper Broadfield car park in Rochdale town centre and spent almost three hours in bars and pubs nearby with three friends.

CCTV operators watching the town centre saw him return to the car at around 3.25am and alerted police that a man who appeared intoxicated was about to drive away. Officers were given a description of the car, its registration and where it was leaving from.

When officers tried to stop the car as it left the town centre, Grainger failed to stop. CCTV showed him driving at speed along Rochdale Road and on the wrong side of the road throughout.

The pursuit ended when a man, now 41, was struck by the police car as officers tried to bring Grainger to a stop. Officers stopped to give him first aid at the scene. GMP said his injuries have changed his life.

Grainger kept driving before abandoning the car on Wellington Street, where CCTV captured him and his three passengers running from it. He was arrested the next day, gave no comment in interview, and was found not to be insured to drive the car. The court ordered the Seat Leon to be destroyed.

One of the passengers, Teagan Clements, later gave police a false statement. She was given a 20-week prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, and 80 hours of unpaid work for making a false statement tendered in evidence.

Detective Sergeant Louise Warhurst, of GMP’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said Grainger had consciously chosen to drive after drinking, and that the injured man’s life had been fundamentally changed.

“This case serves as a stark reminder of the potentially life-changing consequences of drink-driving,” she said.

GMP’s release gives the prison term as “four years and five” without completing the figure. Rochdale Daily has asked the press office to confirm the full term and will update this report.

articles.title: Middleton pupils form giant star to celebrate Rhodes Green school's new name
articles.excerpt: The former Little Heaton primary school welcomed the Bishop of Middleton for a celebration of its new name, with classroom visits, worship and a tree planting.
articles.content_html:
Pupils at a Middleton primary school formed a giant star in their playground to celebrate its new name during a visit from the Bishop of Middleton.

Rhodes Green Church of England Primary School, on Boardman Lane in Rhodes, welcomed the Rt Revd Mark Davies on Thursday 5 November. Children, staff, parents and members of the community joined the celebrations, which included classroom visits, worship and the planting of a commemorative tree.

The school was previously known as Little Heaton CE Primary School. It changed its name in September to reflect its connection with the Rhodes community, where many of its pupils live. Rochdale Council's school directory also records the change.

The star reflected the school's Christian vision, “Shine as stars in the world”, with children lining up in the playground to form its outline for a photograph taken from above.

Headteacher Chloe Noon said: “Rhodes Green is about much more than a new name. It's about the school we're building together and making sure every child feels happy, safe and proud to belong here.”

She added: “We want our children to have big dreams, to believe in themselves and to know that they can achieve wonderful things. Seeing them come together today, and hearing Bishop Mark share that same message, has been really special for all of us.”

The head boy and head girl showed the Bishop around the school, taking him into classrooms to meet children from every year group before an assembly with families. Pupils and staff gave readings during the celebration.

Bishop Mark, who has known the school for more than 20 years, said: “Today has been absolutely amazing and such a tremendous joy and a great blessing. Today represents a new and exciting chapter. A name says so much and is so, so important.”

During a conversation with pupil leaders, he spoke about teachers and church leaders who had encouraged him and urged the children to believe in their own ambitions.

Cranmer Education Trust, which supplied the account of the visit, said the school joined the trust in 2024. Its chief executive Julie Hollis and chair of trustees Janet Gregory attended, alongside the Rev'd Jenni Beaumont from All Saints, Rhodes.

For families who know the school by its former name, Rhodes Green is the same Boardman Lane school. Its current information is available at https://www.rhodesgreen-primary.org/.

Do you have memories of Little Heaton, or a connection with Rhodes Green today? Share them in the comments.

Source: Cranmer Education Trust press release supplied on 6 November 2026, with school name and location checked against Rochdale Council's directory. Photograph: Cranmer Education Trust / supplied.

articles.title: The best beauty salons in Rochdale ranked
articles.excerpt: An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 Google and Fresha reviews.
articles.content_html:
An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 public reviews on Google and Fresha.

The Aesthetic Rooms on Edenfield Road scored 92.6 out of 100, narrowly ahead of Elements Health & Beauty in Newhey on 91.4. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique in Milnrow was third.

Every salon in the top nine is reviewed on both Google and the booking platform Fresha. The town-centre salons with the most Google reviews, led by Pearls on The Walk, take bookings by phone rather than through Fresha, which is why they sit lower down the table.

The top ten

1. The Aesthetic Rooms, Edenfield Road, Norden: 92.6. Google 5.0 from 112 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 372. An aesthetics clinic offering skin treatments, peels and injectables.

2. Elements Health & Beauty, Shaw Road, Newhey: 91.4. Google 5.0 from 108 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 256. A day spa offering massage, facials and head spa treatments.

3. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique, Dale Street, Milnrow: 87.7. Google 4.8 from 43 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 958, the most Fresha reviews of any salon in the table.

4. Be Beau With Grace, Norden: 86.4. Google 4.8 from 44 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 612. Lashes, brows, semi-permanent make-up and training courses.

5. Ella Louise Beautyy, Castleton: 80.1. Google 5.0 from 11 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 130. A home-based nail and beauty studio.

6. ER Beauty Lounge, Halifax Road, Littleborough: 78.0. Google 5.0 from one review; Fresha 5.0 from 730.

7. Beauty by Jemma, Dale Street, Milnrow: 77.0. Google 5.0 from six reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 98.

8. Lush Beauty N Spa, Oldham Road: 75.8. Google 4.7 from 120 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 13.

9. Olivia Bells Clinic, Halifax Road: 75.4. Google 5.0 from 12 reviews; Fresha 4.9 from 44.

10. Cwbeautyofficial, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.6. Fresha 5.0 from 418 reviews; no Google listing found.

The rest of the table

11. NailsByAnabelx, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.3 (Fresha 5.0 from 384; no Google rating).

12. Pearls Hair, Nails & Beauty, The Walk: 47.0 (Google 4.9 from 365, the most Google reviews of any salon in the table; not reviewed on Fresha).

13. Sleek N Chique Beauty & Fashion Salon, Milkstone Place: 45.6 (Google 5.0 from 120).

14. Elegant Beauty and Nails, Sussex Street: 44.8 (Google 5.0 from 97).

15. Nails By Hediye, Yorkshire Street: 41.1 (Google 5.0 from 39).

16. BZ Beauty Studio, Oldham Road: 40.2 (Google 4.8 from 105).

17. Simply Special, Baillie Street: 40.0 (Google 4.9 from 48).

18. Nia Hair & Beauty VIP, Yorkshire Street: 35.8 (Google 4.6 from 128).

How we ranked them

Every figure was taken from the salons' public Google and Fresha listings on Sunday 8 November 2026. No salon was visited, contacted or paid to take part, and none paid to be included.

Each salon could score up to 50 points from Google and up to 50 from Fresha, making 100 in total. Within each half, 30 points are for the star rating and 20 are for the number of reviews.

The rating points are weighted so that a perfect score from a handful of reviews cannot beat a near-perfect score from hundreds. Each salon is treated as if it had 25 extra reviews at the average rating on that platform across the salons in the table: 4.88 stars on Google and 5.00 on Fresha. The more real reviews a salon has, the less those imaginary 25 matter.

The review-count points rise more slowly the more reviews a salon has, so 1,000 reviews is not worth ten times as much as 100. The most-reviewed salon on each platform receives the full 20 points: Pearls on Google, with 365, and Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique on Fresha, with 958.

A salon not reviewed on one of the two platforms scores nothing for that half. That is the single biggest factor in the table. Pearls, for example, earns 47.0 of a possible 50 Google points, more than any other salon, but scores nothing from Fresha. ER Beauty Lounge has only one Google review but 730 on Fresha, and finishes six places higher.

Fresha's reviews come only from customers who booked through it, and almost every salon there holds a perfect 5.0. Its half of the score therefore reflects how many customers book a salon online more than any difference in rating.

Facebook was left out. Follower figures could not be gathered reliably for every salon, and the size of a page's audience says little about the treatment customers receive.

The ranking covers beauty, nail, skin and spa businesses within Rochdale borough. Hair salons will be ranked separately. Salons in Whitworth and Shawforth carry Rochdale postcodes but sit in Rossendale, so they were not included. Home-based studios are named by area only.

Ratings change daily, and this table records them as they stood on 8 November 2026. Salons that believe a figure is wrong can send a correction, with a link to the listing, to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Rochdale's pathology teams support millions of tests during National Pathology Week
articles.excerpt: As National Pathology Week is celebrated, Rochdale's pathology teams highlight their vital role in healthcare, processing over 10 million samples annually.
articles.content_html:
This week marks National Pathology Week, a time to recognise the essential work of pathology teams across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale.

These teams process more than 10 million samples and conduct over 35 million tests each year, playing a crucial role in patient care.

Pathology services are integral to approximately 95% of clinical pathways, providing the diagnostic information that clinicians rely on to diagnose illnesses, guide treatments, and monitor ongoing care. Despite their critical role, many patients may never meet the professionals working behind the scenes in pathology laboratories.

The Northern Care Alliance's pathology workforce includes nearly 700 staff members across various locations, including Rochdale, Oldham, Salford, and Bury. This diverse team comprises biomedical scientists, pathologists, clinical scientists, and other specialists who work together to ensure efficient and accurate testing.

Recent advancements in technology, such as the introduction of automated biopsy processing in Oldham, have improved workflow and increased capacity, allowing biomedical scientists to focus more on specialised diagnostic work.

As the healthcare landscape evolves, the importance of pathology services in supporting patient care continues to grow. The implementation of a new Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) has also transformed how laboratories manage samples and results, ensuring uninterrupted services for patients.

articles.title: Middleton Council completes £3.3 million purchase of Warwick Mill
articles.excerpt: The purchase of Warwick Mill and London House marks a significant step in Middleton's regeneration efforts, with plans for redevelopment underway.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration has taken a significant step forward with the Rochdale Borough Council completing the purchase of Warwick Mill from developer Kam Lei Fong.

The historic cotton mill, built in 1907, has been vacant for over a decade and has become a target for vandalism and urban explorers.

As part of the £3.3 million deal, the council also acquired the neighbouring London House, a 1960s office block that is set to be demolished.

The redevelopment of Warwick Mill is seen as a vital opportunity to restore an important historic building and create new homes for the local community.

Immediate actions include enhancing security at the site with a 24-hour presence from Rochdale firm Winterburns, which will also begin clearing debris, including over 1,000 tyres and overgrown vegetation.

The internal strip-out of both Warwick Mill and London House is expected to commence shortly, with demolition of London House planned for early next year.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed optimism about the redevelopment, stating it will not only improve the area but also provide much-needed housing.

The council will soon begin the process of selecting a developer partner to undertake the long-term redevelopment of Warwick Mill.

articles.title: How many Rochdale servicemen died in the world wars and since? The records give no single answer
articles.excerpt: Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War. No published record gives a borough total for the Second World War or later conflicts.
articles.content_html:
Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War, but no published record gives one total for the borough's war dead.

Rochdale Daily searched the published records on Remembrance Sunday. Different sources give different First World War figures, and none of the sources found gives a borough-wide total for the Second World War or for later conflicts.

First World War

Rochdale Cenotaph, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, was unveiled by the Earl of Derby on 26 November 1922. Public subscription raised £29,443 10s, of which £12,611 paid for the memorial. The rest went to a fund for the families of what were then counted as Rochdale's 2,000 war dead.

A later study puts the figure higher. Real Rochdale magazine, marking the centenary in 2018, reported that "approx 3,000 local men died of the 15,000-16,000 who fought in the war", citing Michael Bull's dissertation "Rochdale and the Great War 1914-1920".

The sources do not say whether the two figures cover the same area.

The north face of the Cenotaph reads: "To the memory of the men of Rochdale who gave their lives in the Great War."

Memorial lists are still being corrected. In 2014, seven names were added to Heywood's First World War memorial: W Parkinson, J McIntyre, B C Butterworth, E Collinge, H Armstrong, J Thornley and H Olden. Their links to the town came to light after relatives researched their family trees.

Second World War

The dates 1939-1945 were added to the Cenotaph after the Second World War, and the sunken garden behind it is the borough's Second World War memorial.

No published total for the borough's Second World War dead was found. Smaller records give part of the picture. The war memorial at Rochdale Cemetery lists 54 names from the Second World War, according to the Manchester and Lancashire Family History Society's transcription.

Rochdale Borough Council's list of war dead commemorated at Rochdale Crematorium names 55 service personnel, who died between 1940 and 1947.

Later conflicts

A bronze plaque on the Cenotaph is dedicated "To all those who died in the service of their country".

Corporal Jack Stanley, 26, of The Queen's Royal Hussars, died in April 2012, more than two months after he was injured by an improvised explosive device on patrol near Lashkar Gah in Helmand, Afghanistan. His mother, Brenda, lives in Littleborough.

She said: "Jack was a kind, generous lad with a ready smile." She added: "The world is duller without him and heaven brighter."

Drummer Lee Rigby, 25, of the 2nd Battalion Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, grew up on the Langley estate in Middleton. He was killed near Woolwich Barracks in south-east London in May 2013.

Finding the names

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission's online database lists service personnel who died in both world wars, and the Imperial War Museums' War Memorials Register records the borough's memorials and many of the names on them.

The council publishes lists of war dead buried in eight of the borough's cemeteries and churchyards, including Heywood, Middleton, Rochdale and Littleborough. Families who believe a relative's name is missing from a memorial can contact the council's armed forces team at ArmedForces@rochdale.gov.uk.

The national two-minute silence for Armistice Day takes place at 11am on Wednesday 11 November.

articles.title: Greater Manchester Police to host pop-up fraud prevention events in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: In a bid to protect shoppers from online fraud, Greater Manchester Police will hold pop-up events in Rochdale next week, providing essential advice and support.
articles.content_html:
In the lead-up to Christmas, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is organising pop-up fraud-prevention events in Rochdale to help shoppers avoid online scams.

The sessions will take place at Virgin Money on Yorkshire Street on Tuesday 10 November, and at Halifax on the same street on Wednesday 11 November, both from 10am to 1pm.

The events are being hosted by GMP’s Economic Crime Unit, which aims to educate the public about the various types of scams, from simple confidence tricks to sophisticated online fraud.

Attendees will have the opportunity to speak with police staff and volunteers about any concerns they may have regarding fraud and cyber crime.

GMP has emphasised the importance of staying informed about the latest scams and has provided tips to reduce the risk of becoming a victim.

These include never sharing passwords or personal details, regularly updating devices and apps, and ensuring that emails and attachments are only opened if they come from trusted sources.

These pop-up events are crucial as they provide direct access to expert advice and support for local residents, particularly during the busy shopping season. By attending, shoppers can better protect themselves from potential scams and ensure a safer festive period.

articles.title: How much will Christmas dinner cost in Rochdale? Lidl's £11.11 deal and how rivals compared
articles.excerpt: Lidl is first to price its 2026 Christmas dinner. Here is how it stacks up against last year's Aldi, Tesco and Morrisons deals for a family of four.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families can buy a basic Christmas dinner for £11.11 at Lidl this year, the first 2026 supermarket price to be announced, with rival deals still to come.

Lidl says its bundle feeds eight for £1.39 a head. For a family of four the shopping list is the same, because the turkey and packs only come in one size, so it works out at about £2.78 each, with leftovers.

The items are on sale in stores from 19 December until Christmas Eve, and Lidl has warned that stock can sell out.

Lidl's basket is a 3kg Birchwood British turkey at £8.85, a 170g pack of sage and onion stuffing at 45p, 15 Yorkshire puddings at 46p and 300g of gravy granules at 99p.

The vegetables are 9p each: 2kg of potatoes, 1kg of carrots, 500g of sprouts and 500g of parsnips. Rochdale Daily has checked that the eight items add up to £11.11.

Aldi, Tesco, Morrisons and M&S had not published their 2026 Christmas dinner prices when this article was written on 8 November. Last year most of them announced in December.

For comparison, here is what each offered in 2025. These are last year's prices, not this year's.

Aldi cut the price of its 2025 dinner for six to £9.31 on 4 December, using the same eight-item list. The turkey was £7.35 and its Super Six vegetables were 5p each. For a family of four that was about £2.33 a head.

Tesco's 2025 dinner for six cost £9.55, but only with a Clubcard. The 3kg turkey was £7.50 with the card, half its usual £5 per kg, and the four vegetables were 15p each. It was sold in most large Tesco stores from 19 December.

Morrisons did not publish a full dinner bundle in 2025. More Card holders could buy carrots, parsnips, sprouts and a swede for 5p each from 18 to 26 December, and 1.5kg of roasting potatoes was £1 for all shoppers.

M&S did not offer a comparable value Christmas dinner, so Rochdale Daily could not price the same basket there.

On last year's prices, Aldi was cheapest without any loyalty card, Tesco came close only for Clubcard holders, and Lidl's opening 2026 price sits £1.80 above Aldi's final 2025 figure.

Loyalty schemes made a real difference in 2025. Tesco's turkey price halved with a Clubcard, and Morrisons' 5p vegetables needed a More Card. Both cards are free to sign up for.

Reduced "yellow sticker" food can also cut the bill. Which? found that Tesco and Morrisons have no set reduction times.

Aldi told Which? that reductions vary by store but are likely near closing time, with fresh food cut by 30% or 75% on its last day. Lidl staff usually reduce items first thing in the morning and a few hours before closing, while M&S reductions are also likely near closing.

Fresh Christmas vegetables and turkeys that reach their date on Christmas Eve are often reduced, but stock is not guaranteed and shoppers relying on it risk going without.

articles.title: Middleton's Veterans' Walk: the poppy mural honouring the town's service men and women on Remembrance Sunday
articles.excerpt: A wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the Middleton in Bloom mural of poppies, a Spitfire and the white cliffs of Dover.
articles.content_html:
A poppy wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the town centre mural that Middleton in Bloom created as a tribute to the town's service men and women, on Remembrance Sunday.

The mural runs the length of a wall in Middleton town centre. A Spitfire trails a stream of red poppies across a painted sky, above silhouettes of soldiers standing among giant poppies, a soldier with a horse, the white cliffs of Dover and a warship at sea.

Planters along the foot of the wall are wrapped in a poppy-print banner carrying the words of Laurence Binyon's poem For the Fallen: "They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old."

The wreath sits beneath the Veterans' Walk plaque, in the planter in front of the painted sea.

The plaque records that the installation was officially opened on 8 May 2025, the 80th anniversary of VE Day, by Ted Woolley OStJ, branch chairman of the Middleton branch of the Royal British Legion.

Middleton in Bloom finished the white cliffs of Dover section in time for VE Day last year, the Rochdale Times reported at the time. The wooden panel had to be replaced, so the sea was painted first and the Spitfire and poppies were added afterwards.

Elsewhere in Middleton, a "Lest We Forget" display of two kneeling soldiers either side of a cross has been planted with red cyclamen and poppies.

Middleton's Remembrance Sunday parade assembled at 10.10am on Long Street this morning and marched to Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road for a service at 10.45am.

More about the group's work is published at middletoninbloom.co.uk.

articles.title: Rochdale Council warns families of confirmed measles cases
articles.excerpt: Families in Rochdale are urged to be vigilant for measles symptoms following confirmed cases, with health officials advising vaccinations.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has issued a warning to families after confirmed cases of measles were reported in the borough. The council highlighted that some of these cases have resulted in visits to Accident and Emergency departments, raising concerns about the potential spread of the virus.

Health officials are advising residents to be aware of the symptoms of measles, which include high fever, runny nose, cough, red and watery eyes, Koplik spots, and a rash that typically starts on the face and spreads across the body.

Measles can lead to serious health complications, particularly for vulnerable individuals such as infants and those with weakened immune systems.

The council has urged parents to ensure their children are vaccinated with the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine, which is usually administered at 12 and 18 months of age.

Those who have not yet received the vaccine are encouraged to contact their GP to arrange an appointment.

This warning serves as a crucial reminder for families in Rochdale about the importance of recognising measles symptoms and ensuring vaccinations are up to date. Vaccination can help prevent the spread of this highly contagious disease.

A spokesperson for EdforAll Ltd stated, "We are committed to working closely with the council to ensure that our hub continues to serve the community effectively." This statement reflects the organisation's intention to maintain its outreach services while adhering to planning requirements.

The need for planning permission underscores the importance of regulatory compliance for community services in Rochdale.

EdforAll Ltd applied to Rochdale Council for a Certificate of Lawfulness for its base at Unit 1, Crown Business Park, in Cowm Top Lane. Documents submitted with the application show it functions as an administrative headquarters for community outreach and a part-time, non-statutory support venue for local schools and young people aged 5 to 18. They add: “The proposed activities do not constitute a ‘school’ or standard educational facility. No change-of-use application is required as the operation aligns with Class E(f) (Day centre) and Class E(g)(i) (Offices). No internal structural changes or external building works are proposed.” It is described as an “intervention partner to local schools, providing short, part-time sessions to help students re-engage with their main education” and functions as a “part-time, non-statutory support venue for local schools and young people” and sessions held there are “intended to prevent school exclusion”, alongside basic literacy, numeracy, or functional skills training. A planning officer’s report said:  “The case officer sought further clarification from the agent regarding the proposed use. The agent clarified that the facility would not be inspected by Ofsted, the Department for Education, or the CQC; and the facility would operate as alternative provision, with placements through referral of the local authority. “Based on the submitted details, further clarification, and the balance of probabilities, the proposed development would fail to meet the statutory definition of a day centre. READ MORE: Lest we forget: Borough falls silent to pay its respects “Firstly, there would be an absence of any care provided at the facility. Academic re-engagement, mentoring, behavioural intervention, and functional skills tutoring of school-aged children does not constitute ‘personal care’ for people in need of such care for reason of old age, disablement, substance dependence, or mental disorder. “Furthermore, the facility would operate as a targeted school intervention partner which would take referrals from the local authority to prevent exclusion and to re-engage registered pupils with their mainstream education. “Parents or the general public do not appear to be able to access the provision without local authority or school referral. A closed, referral-based educational intervention service operating in partnership with local school does not constitute a facility open ‘principally to visiting members of the public’ as required by Class E(f). “Part-time educational re-engagement, functional skills, literacy/numeracy tuition, and school exclusion intervention for 5 to 18 year olds clearly exhibits the primary characteristics of the provision of education under Class F.1(a). Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposed use of the premises as a youth outreach hub and day session centre falls within Use Class E(f) of Schedule 2, Part A of the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987 (as amended). “Specifically, the evidence submitted has not demonstrated that the proposed day session centre would operate in a manner consistent with the meanings and characteristics of that Use Class. “The local planning authority therefore considers that the proposal would result in a material change of use of the land, comprising development within the meaning of section 55(1) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, for which express grant of planning permission is required.” In order to continue operating the outreach hub and day centre, a planning application seeking change of use must be submitted to the council. articles.title: Middleton residents warned about scammers posing as council officials
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has issued a warning to residents in Middleton about scammers posing as council officials to gain entry into homes.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Middleton are being warned about scammers posing as council officials in an attempt to gain entry into their homes. This warning follows reports of several incidents in the area, prompting Rochdale Council to take action.

The council stated, "We have been made aware of bogus cold callers posing as council officers to gain entry into homes." They emphasised that all legitimate council staff carry identification and can produce it upon request.

Residents are advised to check for ID before allowing anyone into their homes.

If residents are unsure about a caller's identity or if they cannot produce an official badge, they are encouraged to refuse entry.

The council also reminded residents that services and appointments can only be booked and paid for in advance through their contact centre at 01706 647474.

Residents who have experienced similar visits are urged to report them to Greater Manchester Police, either online or by calling 101.

articles.title: Castleton Remembrance Sunday service draws big crowd but resident asks for a better speaker next year
articles.excerpt: Crowds gathered on Castleton's village green for the Act of Remembrance, but one resident said the words could not be heard.
articles.content_html:
A large crowd gathered on Castleton's village green for the Remembrance Sunday service this morning, but one resident said nobody could hear what was being said.

Castleton's Act of Remembrance began at 10.50am at Castleton Memorial Gardens on Queensway, on the village green. The service was led by St Martin's Parish Church, according to the order of service handed to those attending.

Photographs from the service show people lining the green as the service took place under the trees.

Writing in the Castleton community group on Facebook after the service, Graham Glover said: "Great turnout but please can we invest in a new speaker for next year? You can't hear a word being said."

Castleton's service was one of eight Remembrance Sunday parades and services held across the Rochdale borough today, in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle.

Armistice Day falls on Wednesday 11 November, with the national two-minute silence at 11am.

articles.excerpt: Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his home in Rochdale, which has raised concerns among local planners.
articles.content_html:
Lewis Mahoney has applied for retrospective planning permission for a new garden wall and fencing at his property located at 1 Bates Close, Rochdale.

The application has sparked discussions among local planners regarding the impact of the new structure on the character of the surrounding area.

Planners have expressed concerns that the new fencing is out of character with the existing street scene, which typically features low-rise fencing and lacks hard boundary treatments.

This has led to a debate about how the new installation fits within the established aesthetic of Bates Close.

The planning committee is currently reviewing the application and considering the implications of the new wall and fencing on the neighbourhood's visual coherence.

The outcome of this review will determine whether the retrospective permission will be granted or if the structure will need to be modified or removed.

This case highlights the ongoing challenges residents face when making changes to their properties in ways that may not align with local planning guidelines. The decision will be significant for Mahoney and could set a precedent for similar applications in the area.

articles.excerpt: St James Place on Yorkshire Street will be transformed into residential apartments after sitting empty for eight years, with planning permission granted for the redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
A former office block in Rochdale will be converted into 21 new apartments after sitting empty for nearly a decade.

St James Place, located on Yorkshire Street, has received planning permission from Rochdale Council for the redevelopment, which aims to provide much-needed housing in the area.

Developer Alam Investments plans to create a mix of one and two-bedroom flats, each featuring its own living, dining, and kitchen space. The project is described as a 'sensitive and appropriate reuse of the building', with only internal changes planned to the structure.

A heritage statement was required for the application due to the proximity of the Grade II-listed St Mary’s Ukrainian Catholic Church.

The planning documents noted that the building has been vacant for approximately eight years and is in need of investment and reuse, stating that the proposed scheme will contribute positively to the vitality and regeneration of Rochdale town centre.

This redevelopment is seen as a significant step towards addressing the housing shortage in the area, providing residents with modern living spaces in a sustainable location. The project is expected to enhance the local community and support ongoing regeneration efforts in Rochdale.

Rochdale Borough Council has announced its support for the Greater Manchester Good Landlord Charter, which seeks to elevate standards in the private rented sector. This initiative aims to ensure that privately rented homes are safer, better managed, and fairer for tenants.

The Charter outlines standards that exceed legal requirements, encouraging landlords to provide well-maintained properties. Landlords can join the Charter for free, starting as supporters and working towards full membership by demonstrating compliance with the established standards.

By signing up, landlords commit to enhancing the quality of rental properties, which directly benefits tenants by ensuring safer living conditions. The Council encourages residents to check if their landlords are participating in the Charter, promoting accountability in the rental market.

This initiative is significant for local residents as it aims to improve the overall quality of housing in Rochdale, making it a more attractive place to live. For more information about the Good Landlord Charter, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Bikers in red leave Birch Services for 13th Ring of Red ride around the M60
articles.excerpt: Riders were due to set off from the M62 services at 1pm to form a giant poppy around Manchester, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.
articles.content_html:
Bikers in red were due to leave Birch Services on the M62 at 1pm today for the 13th Ring of Red ride, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.

Riders gather at the westbound HGV parking area of the services, which sit between Heywood and Middleton, before heading along the M62 and joining the M60 at junction 18.

They then travel clockwise around the whole of Manchester's ring road. With every rider wearing something red, the procession is meant to look like a giant poppy encircling the city when seen from above.

Riders could gather from 8am, and organisers said the westbound lorry park would be closed to HGVs from Saturday night until 2.30pm today. More than 1,000 motorcyclists were expected.

Jeanette "Netty" Kiely, who organises Ring of Red M60, told Roch Valley Radio the ride was a way of saying "we remember, we care, and we will never forget".

Ms Kiely said seeing the bikes come together each year reminded organisers why they do it. She also praised the Bridge Supporters who stand on motorway bridges in all weathers to wave and cheer as the riders pass underneath.

She added that after 13 years the event had become a community coming together to remember, rather than simply a motorcycle ride.

The Ride of Respect is free to join and non-competitive. It honours members of the Armed Forces past and present and those who died in service.

Money is raised through sales of official red T-shirts, hoodies and patches, with a separate clothing range for Bridge Supporters. Heywood Veterans Association, this year's nominated charity, supports veterans in Heywood, Middleton and surrounding areas.

The Manchester ride grew out of the original Ring of Red on the M25. Ms Kiely has previously said she agreed to stage a northern version after a phone call from the London organiser.

The M60 event's biggest turnout came in 2022, when 5,986 bikes took part, up from 4,400 the year before. Ms Kiely said at the time: "It was incredible to have our highest turn out yet – with 5986 bikes."

Around 3,000 bikers took part last year, according to the Oldham Times. Previous nominated charities include Veterans into Logistics and Veterans in Communities.

Riders finish back at Birch Services once the lap of the M60 is complete.

Source: Ring of Red M60 organisers via Roch Valley Radio. Photograph: supplied.

articles.title: Rochdale care leaver behind Little Acts of Christmas explains why no young person should go without a gift
articles.excerpt: Brianna, who grew up in care, started Little Acts of Christmas to give presents to young people in care. Her appeal has passed £900, with more than 30 requests so far.
articles.content_html:
A young Rochdale care leaver has explained why she started Little Acts of Christmas, an independent appeal to make sure children and teenagers in care do not go without a present this Christmas.

Brianna, who grew up in the care system herself, set up the project to provide gifts for young people aged roughly 10 to 18 who are in care, care-experienced or otherwise at risk of missing out. She runs it alone, without a charity, staff or budget behind her, and has built it largely through TikTok alongside a GoFundMe page and an Amazon wishlist.

In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, Brianna said: "Christmas is often portrayed as a magical time of year, but for some children and young people, it can be a reminder of the things they don't have, the people they might be missing or the difficult circumstances they're growing up in."

She added: "I didn't want to just sit back and accept that some young people might go without Christmas presents or that they might feel forgotten. Instead, I wanted to do something about it."

Brianna said young people in care, and those leaving it, can feel increasingly overlooked as they get older, and that she wanted to turn her own experience into something positive for others.

"I'm not a big organisation, I don't have a team of employees or a large budget behind me. I'm simply someone who understands how important even the smallest act of kindness can be," she said.

The appeal set out to raise £800 to buy gifts for more than 50 young people. On 2 November it stood at £140, with more than 12 young people having already messaged Brianna through TikTok to ask whether they could receive a present.

Since then the total has risen sharply. Brianna told Rochdale Daily that the appeal had passed £900 by Saturday 7 November, including a £700 donation from a business whose owner is himself a former care leaver.

Requests have grown too, to more than 30. Brianna said she has paused new requests until Thursday 12 November so that she does not promise gifts she cannot deliver. She plans to go shopping that day for the 30 young people already on her list, and will reopen requests if enough money remains.

She also has to cover postage, as she wants the project to reach young people beyond Rochdale.

Brianna is asking for financial donations, brand-new gifts, support from local businesses and organisations, or simply for people to share the fundraiser. She hopes to grow Little Acts of Christmas into a larger initiative across Greater Manchester and beyond, possibly as an independent organisation in future.

"A present might seem like a small thing to some people, but to someone who isn't expecting anything, knowing that somebody has thought about them can mean so much more than the gift itself," she said.

Donations can be made through the Little Acts of Christmas GoFundMe page at gofund.me/be1e51022, and the project can be found on TikTok at @Littleactsofchristmas.

Have you been helped by a project like this, or could your business support the appeal? Let us know in the comments.

Tesco declined to comment on the incident when approached by the media.

This incident underscores the critical role of emergency services in responding to health crises. Local readers are encouraged to remain aware of community support services and safety measures.

articles.title: Who is the 'Sad Cavalier' said to haunt Middleton's Ring O'Bells?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.body:
If you ask pub regulars and local guidebooks who the Ring O'Bells' ghost is, they'll give you a tidy answer: the Sad Cavalier, nicknamed Edward, a Royalist in plumed hat and cloak who haunts the old inn and its cellars. That account — a betrayed cavalier fleeing through a secret tunnel, murdered at a church exit, and buried under the pub's flagstones — is the version most often repeated in tourism and folklore write-ups, and it is the story behind ghost-hunt events now advertised for the building on St Leonard's Square. (Visit Rochdale’s local history/what’s-on page summarises the tradition in full.)

But legend and archive are not the same thing. What survives in contemporary and older printed sources is two separate threads: first, Middleton's documented seventeenth‑century politics and local gentry; second, a body of later folklore, local recollections and modern tourism copy that stitches a named cavalier to the Ring O'Bells. The reliable historical picture is straightforward: Middleton and its leading families were active in the Civil Wars and, as local histories explain, many local men and some gentry supported Parliament. Nineteenth‑century accounts of the town (for example, Edwin Waugh’s Lancashire Sketches) record Ralph Assheton and others raising men for the parliamentary cause and the wider county’s contested loyalties in the 1640s. Those sources show the town was very much a theatre of seventeenth‑century political division — which makes it an easy setting for a Royalist-versus-Roundhead ghost story.

The Stannycliffe name that appears in the Ring O'Bells tale also exists in the documentary record. County and diocesan antiquarian material mention a house or hall near Middleton called Stannycliffe (older printed collections record people “of Stannycliffe Hall” and deaths there). Those references confirm Stannycliffe as a historic local place‑name and social unit, not a modern invention of ghost tours. They do not, however, identify an “Edward” who was killed at the pub or provide a contemporary 1640s account of the gruesome ambush the legend describes.

What the tradition adds — and what we cannot yet verify from primary records — are the grisly details: a secret tunnel linking the Ring O'Bells' cellar to St Leonard’s church; the discovery of Civil War‑period pikes, buckles or helmets beneath the cellar flagstones; several skeletons dug up and identified as seventeenth century; and a 1972 newspaper report of violent cellar phenomena. These claims are regularly echoed in guidebooks and paranormal sites and are summarised on Visit Rochdale’s event listing, but I could not locate a contemporary archaeological report, museum accession record or an accessible copy of the cited 1972 Oldham Evening Chronicle item while researching this piece. In short: the colourful physical evidence cited in the story appears in modern folklore sources, but I found no published excavation report or council record confirming human remains or a formal 17th‑century burial under the pub.

That distinction matters for readers: Middleton’s seventeenth‑century division and the existence of Stannycliffe give the story a historically plausible frame, but plausibility is not proof. If you want to pursue the matter further, the borough’s Local Studies and Archives holds parish registers, newspapers, maps and estate papers that are the right places to look for contemporary mentions (the Rochdale Local Studies Centre and Middleton library collections are the starting points listed by the council). A verified archaeological report or an indexed newspaper copy would settle whether the cellar finds and the 1972 incidents are documentary facts or later accretions to the tale.

So who is the Sad Cavalier? In Middleton today he is, quite plainly, a figure of folk memory: a Royalist gentleman named in local story, given the friendly if mournful nickname Edward by landlords and guide‑writers. The deeper, verifiable facts are less dramatic — a documented history of local Parliamentary activity in the 1640s and the historic place‑name Stannycliffe — and no clear primary record tying a named Royalist corpse to the Ring O'Bells' cellar has been located in the sources checked for this piece. The legend will keep drawing in curiosity; for readers who prefer evidence to atmosphere, the archives at Touchstones/Rochdale Local Studies and the parish papers are where the next, verifiable chapter would appear.

Sources consulted: Visit Rochdale’s Ring O'Bells entry and event listing for the pub’s folklore; nineteenth‑century local histories recording Middleton’s Civil War activity; and diocesan/antiquarian material that attests to a historic Stannycliffe near Middleton. Where modern guides repeat finds of helmets, pikes and skeletons beneath the cellar I have flagged those claims as unverified pending archival or archaeological confirmation.

articles.title: Is there really a secret tunnel under Middleton between the Ring O’Bells and St Leonard’s?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.body:
Short answer: no published, verifiable evidence has been found that a continuous built tunnel links the Ring O’Bells (St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

The story is older and more persistent than the proof. For generations Middleton guides, ghost‑tour pages and regional folklore compilations have repeated a neat Civil War image: Royalists meet in the pub cellar, a hidden passage runs under the road to the church and the plotters slip away when the Roundheads arrive. The tale is still used on commercial ghost walks and local history roundups. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Where the legend runs into trouble is the documentary and professional heritage record. St Leonard’s is a Grade I listed medieval church whose National Heritage List entry sets out its fabric, phases and sensitivity in detail; that entry makes no mention of a connecting passage. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332)) The Middleton Town Centre conservation‑area appraisal kept by Rochdale Council, the document that describes known historic assets and archaeological sensitivity across the square, likewise does not record any mapped or scheduled tunnel between the buildings. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/6313525))

Stories of bones, buckles, muskets and a landlord frightened by a flying stone appear repeatedly in popular accounts and in later retellings of a local newspaper item often cited as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972. Those secondary sources show how the tale has been told and retold, but I could not find a publicly accessible archaeological report, museum accession entry or digitised press copy that records the 1972 item or the claimed finds to the standard used by heritage professionals. In short: there are repeated claims of finds in folklore and tourism material, and an absence of a published excavation report or archive catalogue entry to corroborate them. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

That absence matters. If a brick‑lined or purpose‑built passage had been known, recorded or opened in modern times it would normally appear in at least one of these places: the national listing or schedule, the local conservation appraisal, an archaeological trust report, or a museum accession catalogue for recovered artefacts. None of those formal records I checked lists a continuous tunnel between the pub and the church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Does that mean there was no subterranean connection at any point in any century? Not necessarily. Old cellars, drains, short escape routes and rubble‑filled voids are common in historic town centres; people over the centuries may have used cellars and alleys in ways oral tradition remembers as a “tunnel”. The distinction between an occasional informal route (a bricked‑up opening, a man‑hole, a drainage culvert) and an intentionally constructed, continuous tunnel is crucial and is where legend and archaeological standards part company. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

If a reader wants to move the story from local memory to proof, the practical steps are straightforward. Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection. The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past. That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents. Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection.

The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past.

That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents.

Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))
